a: Of Asaph
t: The Asaph psalms, and how this part is numbered
p: Psalms 50 and 73–83 carry Asaph's name. Hebrew Bibles count each title as verse 1, so their numbers run one higher.
b: Asaph was one of the three Levite song leaders Chronicles names under David (1 Chronicles 15:17, 19; 16:5), and "the sons of Asaph" sang at the Temple long after (Ezra 2:41). Twelve psalms bear his name, eleven of them here in Book III (73–83); Psalm 83 is the last. Scholars note that they mention Joseph, Ephraim and the exodus more than other psalms, and many trace them to singers from the northern tribes (see 81:5). Numbering: in Hebrew Bibles a psalm's title is verse 1, so 81:1 here is 81:2 there, and so on through Psalm 89. The Greek and Latin also number the psalms themselves one lower in this stretch: Psalm 81 is their Psalm 80, and Psalm 89 is their 88.

a: On the gittith
t: Gittith: a lyre from Gath, or a winepress song?
p: The word is unexplained. The Targum says a lyre from Gath; the Greek read "for the winepresses".
b: Gittit stands in three titles (8:0; 81:0; 84:0). It looks like a feminine form of Gath, the Philistine city, and the Targum explains it as "the lyre that came from Gath", an instrument or tuning David may have brought back from his years there (1 Samuel 27). The Greek and Jerome's Gallican Latin read gittot, "winepresses" (hyper tōn lēnōn, pro torcularibus), which would make it a vintage song. That fits Psalm 81 well, since the autumn Feast of Booths came at the end of the grape harvest. No reading is certain, so the Plain keeps the word.

a: play the pleasant lyre and the harp
p: The tof was a hand drum, the kinnor a small lyre, and the nevel a larger, deeper stringed instrument.
b: The tof was a frame drum held in one hand and beaten with the other, the instrument of Miriam (Exodus 15:20). The kinnor was the lyre David played (1 Samuel 16:23), a light frame with strings, often shown in ancient art held at an angle. The nevel was probably a larger lyre or harp with a deeper sound. Lyres of this kind are pictured on reliefs and seals from Egypt to Mesopotamia. The call to strike up the music shows a festival crowd, not a quiet prayer.

a: blow the ram's horn
t: The shofar at the new moon
p: The shofar is a ram's horn trumpet. Jews still sound it on Rosh Hashanah, and this verse is the reason most often given.
b: The shofar was a curved ram's horn, blown for signals, war and worship, not for melody. The Law tells Israel to sound trumpets "on the first day of each month" (Numbers 10:10) and calls the first day of the seventh month "a reminder made with loud blasts" (Leviticus 23:24). The Talmud reads this verse as the command for that day, Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 8a–b), and synagogues still read 81:3–4 at the festival. The Targum agrees: "Blow the shofar in the month of Tishri."

a: at the full moon, when our feast day comes
p: Keseh is rare. It probably means the full moon of Booths; the rabbis took it as the hidden moon of the new year.
b: The word keseh appears only here and in Proverbs 7:20. Phoenician ks' and Syriac kesa mean the full moon (Tate), so most scholars read: blow at the new moon (the first of the seventh month) and at the full moon (the fifteenth), when the Feast of Booths began (Leviticus 23:34). The Talmud heard kasah, "cover": the feast "on which the moon is covered", that is, the new moon of Rosh Hashanah. The Greek has "on the well-marked day". Either way the psalm belongs to the great autumn festival season, and "our feast day" (chag) usually means Booths.

a: a ruling from the God of Jacob
p: Mishpat means a ruling. Jewish tradition heard "judgment" and made Rosh Hashanah the day God judges the world.
b: Mishpat is the word for a legal ruling or a judgment. In the context it simply means a festival rule given by God. But the Talmud reads the two verses together: blow the shofar on the new moon, "for it is a rule for Israel, a judgment of the God of Jacob". From this it concludes that Rosh Hashanah is the day of judgment, when all who come into the world pass before God (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 8a–b; Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2). That idea shapes the Jewish High Holy Days to this day.

a: He made it a decree in Joseph
p: Joseph stands for all Israel, or the northern tribes. The spelling here, Yehosef, is found nowhere else.
b: The name is written Yehosef, with the extra letter of God's name, a spelling found only here. Joseph stands for the people whose fathers went down to Egypt, and often for the northern tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh (77:15; 78:67; 80:1). The Asaph psalms use these northern names more than others do, and many scholars think they began with northern singers, perhaps at Bethel, and were brought south to Jerusalem after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Others take Joseph here simply as a poetic name for all Israel.

a: when he went out over the land of Egypt
p: The exact phrase is used of Joseph in Genesis 41:45. In the psalm "he" is most likely God, going out against Egypt.
b: Genesis uses these very words of Joseph: "And Joseph went out over the land of Egypt" (Genesis 41:45), when Pharaoh made him ruler. The Talmud links them and says Joseph left prison on Rosh Hashanah (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 10b–11a). Most modern readers take "he" as God, who "went out" through Egypt on the night of the exodus (Exodus 11:4), so the festival recalls the night Israel was set free. The Hebrew preposition 'al can mean "over" or "against"; the Greek simply has "out of the land of Egypt".

a: I hear a speech I had never known
p: The line introduces the speech that follows. Readers differ over who hears it and why it is strange.
b: Literally "a lip I did not know I hear". Three readings are common. (1) A prophet or Levite in the Temple speaks: in worship he hears an unfamiliar voice, God's own oracle, which begins in the next verse. Many scholars think a cult prophet delivered such words at the festival. (2) Israel is the speaker: in Egypt it heard a language it did not understand, as in 114:1. (3) Jewish tradition says Joseph heard and learned Pharaoh's languages, and the Targum renders "a language I did not know, I learned"; the Talmud says Gabriel taught him seventy tongues (Bavli Sotah 36b). The Greek has "he heard".

a: his palms let go of the basket
p: The dud was a basket or pot. Egyptian paintings show slaves carrying clay and bricks in such baskets.
b: God recalls the forced labor of Exodus 1:11–14: making bricks and carrying loads. The dud can be a pot or a basket. The Targum and Rashi took it as a cooking pot or kiln; most modern readers think of the baskets in which workers carried mud and bricks. A wall painting in the tomb of Rekhmire, a vizier of Thebes about 1450 BC, shows foreign workers making bricks and carrying them in exactly this way. The Greek renders "his hands served in the basket".

a: hidden in the thunder
p: God answered from the thunder: Sinai, where the people heard his voice from the cloud.
b: "The hiding place of thunder" recalls Sinai, where "there was thunder and flashes of lightning, a heavy cloud on the mountain" (Exodus 19:16), and Moses went up close to "the deep darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21). God's answer came out of the storm cloud that hid him. The order here is the story's order: slavery, the cry, the rescue, Sinai, then the testing in the desert.

a: At the waters of Meribah I put you to the test
p: At Meribah Israel tested God. Here God says he was testing Israel, as Deuteronomy 33:8 also says.
b: Meribah means "quarreling". In Exodus the people "put the LORD on trial" there, asking whether he was with them at all (Exodus 17:7); in Numbers it is the place "where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD" (Numbers 20:13). The psalm turns the story around: God was the one doing the testing, to see whether Israel would trust him. Moses' blessing of Levi says the same, "whom you tested at Massah" (Deuteronomy 33:8). Psalm 95, another festival psalm with a divine warning, uses Meribah the same way (95:8–9).

a: No strange god is to be among you
t: The first of the Ten Words
p: Verses 9–10 repeat the start of the Ten Words: no other god, "I am the LORD your God".
b: God's warning is the heart of the covenant: "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, that house of slaves" (Exodus 20:2), followed by the ban on other gods. Scholars point out that festivals were where Israel heard the covenant read again (Deuteronomy 31:10–13 commands it at Booths every seventh year). Psalms 50 and 81, both of Asaph, sound like such a renewal. Zar "strange" and nekhar "foreign" are the usual words for gods from outside Israel (Deuteronomy 32:12, 16).

a: who brought you up from the land of Egypt
p: Exodus 20:2 has "brought you out". "Brought you up" is what the golden calf was said to have done.
b: Exodus 20:2 says God "brought you out" (hotse'tikha). The psalm uses "brought you up" (hamma'alkha), the very phrase the people used of the golden calf: "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt" (Exodus 32:4), and the phrase Jeroboam used of the calves he set up at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28). If the Asaph psalms come from northern singers, the choice may be pointed: the LORD, not a calf, brought Israel up.

a: Open your mouth as wide as you can, and I will fill it
p: Like a chick with its beak open, Israel is told to ask big. God promises to fill it, as he did with manna.
b: The picture is of a nestling stretching its beak for food. God, who fed Israel in the desert, offers more than they dare to ask. The line looks back to the manna and forward to verse 16. Some scholars think it once stood after verse 5 or at the end and was moved; the versions all have it here. Christian readers have heard in it an invitation to ask boldly in prayer (Ephesians 3:20) and to receive Christ in the Eucharist.

a: the stubbornness of their hearts
t: Handed over to their own hearts
p: Sherirut lev is Deuteronomy's and Jeremiah's word for a hardened will. God's judgment is to let people have their way.
b: Sherirut lev, "stubbornness of heart", appears in Deuteronomy 29:19 and eight times in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:24; 9:14; 11:8). Here God's punishment is not fire or plague but release: he lets Israel go where it insists on going. Paul describes God's judgment the same way: three times in Romans 1 "God gave them over" to what they wanted (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

a: Oh, if my people were listening to me
p: God speaks like a parent who wishes things had gone otherwise. Readers debate what that says about human choice.
b: The Hebrew lu expresses a wish that has not come true. God does not threaten; he grieves, and promises what he would still do (verses 14–16). Jewish readers heard in this a call to return that is never withdrawn. Christian readers compare Jesus over Jerusalem: "How many times I wanted to gather your children close" (Matthew 23:37). The verse is often cited in debates about free will: Arminian and Wesleyan writers take it as proof that God's will can be resisted, while Reformed writers distinguish God's revealed wish from his secret decree.

a: would come cringing to him
p: Kichesh means to lie or feign. Defeated enemies would pretend loyalty, as in 18:44.
b: The verb kichesh usually means "deceive" or "deny". Of a defeated enemy it means to cringe and flatter, offering a submission that is not meant, as foreigners come cringing to the king in 18:44 (the same verse as 2 Samuel 22:45). The Greek translates it "they lied to him". The picture is of a world where even the LORD's enemies have to bow, whether they mean it or not.

a: and their time would last forever
p: The Hebrew says only "their time". It may be the enemies' doom or Israel's good time.
b: 'Ittam, "their time", has no clear owner. If "they" are the LORD's haters, their time of punishment would never end. If "they" are Israel, mentioned in verse 13, their time of blessing would last forever, which suits verse 16. The Greek and Latin keep the ambiguity. Rashi took it as the enemies' time of retribution, lasting forever; the Targum has "their strength will last forever" (both checked myself). The Plain keeps the open wording.

a: He would feed him with the best of the wheat
p: "The fat of the wheat" and "honey from the rock" come from Deuteronomy 32, where God feeds Israel in the land.
b: The Hebrew is "the fat of the wheat", the richest grain. Both images come from the Song of Moses: "He let him suck honey from the rock / and oil from hard flint" and "the plumpest kernels of wheat" (Deuteronomy 32:13–14). Honey from a rock may mean wild bees' honey in rock clefts, or simply plenty in an unlikely place. The switch from "he" to "I" in this verse is in the Hebrew; the Greek makes both lines "he" (see the variant).

a: the best of the wheat
t: "Cibavit eos": a hymn for the Eucharist
p: In the Latin, this verse opens the Mass of Corpus Christi.
b: The Latin of this verse, Cibavit eos ex adipe frumenti, et de petra melle saturavit eos ("He fed them with the fat of the wheat, and with honey from the rock he filled them"), is the entrance chant (Introit) of the Catholic feast of Corpus Christi, the feast of the Body of Christ. Christian readers took the wheat as the eucharistic bread and the rock as Christ, following Paul: "the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Jewish reading stays with the land: the wheat and honey of the promised land if Israel will listen.

a: A psalm of Asaph.
p: Levites sang Psalm 82 in the Temple every Tuesday. Jews still say it as the psalm of the day on Tuesdays.
b: The Mishnah lists the psalm the Levites sang each day of the week at the daily offering: 24 on Sunday, 48 on Monday, 82 on Tuesday, 94 on Wednesday, 81 on Thursday, 93 on Friday and 92 on the Sabbath (Mishnah Tamid 7:4). Both psalms of this section's opening pair were part of that cycle. The Talmud explains Tuesday's choice: on the third day of creation God revealed the dry land, and here he stands to judge it (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a). The Jewish prayer book keeps the cycle.

a: God takes his stand
p: In Psalms 42–83 "God" usually replaces the name YHWH. The one who stands up to judge is Israel's God.
b: Psalms 42–83 are called the Elohistic Psalter, because in them Elohim ("God") appears far more than the name YHWH ("the LORD"), the reverse of the rest of the Psalter. Compare Psalm 14 and 53, the same psalm with "the LORD" and "God" (see 53:0). Many think an editor replaced the name here, so the judge standing in the council is the LORD himself. Nitsav means to take one's stand, as a judge rising to give a verdict: "The LORD takes his place to accuse" (Isaiah 3:13, the same verb).

a: in the assembly of El
p: 'Adat-el is "the assembly of El" or "the divine assembly". At Ugarit, El was the head of a council of gods.
b: 'Edah is the word for Israel's assembly. El means "God", but it is also the name of the high god of the Canaanite texts from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), who sits as king over "the assembly of the gods" and "the sons of El". Israel's poets called the LORD by the name El, and many scholars think the psalm pictures the LORD presiding in the council once imagined around El, or rising in that council against the other gods. The Greek and Latin read "the assembly of gods"; Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew has "the assembly of God"; the Targum turns it into "the assembly of the righteous who are strong in the Law".

a: among the gods he passes judgment
p: Three main answers: heavenly beings who rule the nations, human judges, or Israel at Sinai.
b: Heavenly beings. Most scholars, and many evangelical writers such as Michael Heiser, read elohim as members of God's council, the "sons of God" to whom the nations were handed (Deuteronomy 32:8). They rule unjustly, so God sentences them to die. This fits "the assembly of El" and the threat that they will die "as humans die". Human judges. The Targum, Rashi, Midrash Tehillim, Calvin and Luther take the gods as Israel's judges and rulers, called elohim because they act for God (compare Exodus 22:8–9, where a case comes "before God"). Israel at Sinai. The Talmud reads verse 6 of Israel receiving the Law, made immortal and then losing it at the golden calf (Bavli Avodah Zarah 5a). Some read John 10:34–36 this way too.

a: God takes his stand in the assembly of El
p: A Dead Sea Scroll read this verse as a prophecy of Melchizedek judging Belial and his spirits.
b: In 11QMelchizedek, a Qumran text copied in the first century BC, the first line of this psalm is applied to Melchizedek, a heavenly deliverer: he is the Elohim who "stands in the assembly of El" and judges in the midst of the gods. Verse 2, "How long will you give crooked rulings", is turned against Belial and the spirits of his lot. The text joins the psalm to Isaiah 61 and the year of release in Leviticus 25. It shows that some Jews before Jesus already read Psalm 82 as a scene of heavenly judgment. Compare the priest-king Melchizedek in Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 7.

a: How long will you give crooked rulings
p: To "lift the face" of someone is to favor him. The Law forbade it in court, and God himself never does it.
b: "Lift the faces of the wicked" (pene resha'im tis'u) is the idiom for showing favoritism, like judging by who a person is instead of what he did. The Law forbids it: "Do not lift up the face of the poor man, and do not honor the face of the great man" (Leviticus 19:15). Of God himself Deuteronomy says, "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). The gods are charged with the very thing God refuses to do. "How long" ('ad matai) is the cry of the lament psalms, here spoken by God himself.

a: Judge for the weak and the orphan
t: What gods and kings were supposed to do
p: Across the ancient Near East, kings and gods claimed to defend the widow and orphan. Here gods are judged for failing.
b: Hammurabi's law stone (about 1750 BC) says he was called "so that the strong might not oppress the weak" and to give justice to the orphan and widow. In the Ugaritic story of King Kirta, his son accuses him: "You do not judge the widow's case, you do not try the case of the wretched" (KTU 1.16 vi, paraphrased). So the standard is shared. What is new in Psalm 82 is that the gods themselves are put on trial by that standard, and lose. Israel's Law makes the same demand of every judge (Deuteronomy 24:17) and of the king (72:2–4).

a: Every foundation of the earth totters
p: When judges fail, the whole created order wobbles. Justice holds the world up.
b: In biblical thought the earth stands on foundations God laid (Job 38:4–6; 104:5), and justice is part of that order. When the powers that should keep justice do not, the world itself shakes. Compare 11:3, where the foundations are torn down, and 75:3, where God holds up the earth's pillars. "They do not know, and they do not understand" may describe the gods, blind to the harm they cause, or the oppressed, who stumble in the dark because no one judges for them.

a: I said, 'You are gods
t: "I said": a decree, or a thought?
p: Ani amarti can mean "I declared" or "I had thought". Either way God now takes it back.
b: "I said" (ani amarti) can introduce a decree: I appointed you gods. It can also mean "I had thought" (as in 31:22, where the speaker said in alarm that he was cut off), and then the next verse corrects it: I thought you were gods, but you will die like humans. Rashi follows the Sinai reading: "When I gave you the Law, I gave it on condition that the angel of death would not rule over you." The Targum softens the words: "Like angels you are counted." The verse is the one Jesus quotes in John 10:34.

a: sons of the Most High
p: The gods are "sons of Elyon", members of God's court, the beings Deuteronomy 32:8 says received the nations.
b: Elyon, "Most High", is an old title of God (Genesis 14:18–19). The "sons of God" are the members of his heavenly court in Job (Job 1:6) and in the Song of Moses, where the Most High divided the nations "to match the number of the sons of God" (Deuteronomy 32:8). That reading of Deuteronomy follows a Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek; the traditional Hebrew has "sons of Israel". Read together, the two passages tell a story: God handed the nations to these beings, and in Psalm 82 he takes the nations back because they failed.

a: You are gods
p: Accused of making himself God, Jesus answers from this verse: Scripture itself calls others "gods".
b: In John 10:33–36 the crowd says Jesus, a man, makes himself God. He answers: "Your own law has it written, doesn't it, 'I said, You are gods'? So, if he called those people gods, the people the word of God came to, and the Scripture cannot be undone, then the one the Father made holy and sent into the world, do you say to him, 'You blaspheme,' because I said, 'I am God's Son'?" (John 10:34–36). The argument runs from lesser to greater. "The people the word of God came to" suits the Sinai reading (Israel receiving the Law) or the judges reading; scholars such as Neyrey argue John used the Sinai tradition. Jesus calls the psalm "law" in the broad sense of Scripture.

a: Yet you will die as humans die
p: Ke'adam can mean "like humans" or "like Adam". Jerome, Rashi and the Midrash took it as Adam.
b: Ke'adam is "like a human" or "like Adam". Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew renders "you will die like Adam" (quasi Adam moriemini), and Rashi explains: like Adam you will die, because you corrupted your deeds as he did. Midrash Tehillim tells it as a story: God gave the first man one command, he broke it and was driven from the garden. On the heavenly reading, the sentence is a demotion: beings who were not supposed to die become mortal. On the human reading, judges who thought themselves above the law are reminded that they are dust.

a: you will fall like any one of the princes
p: Sar "prince" is the word Daniel uses for the angel-princes of Persia and Greece. Isaiah pictures stars that fall.
b: Sar means a prince or commander. Daniel uses it for the heavenly "prince of Persia" and "prince of Greece" who oppose God's messenger, and for Michael, "your prince" (Daniel 10:13, 20–21). Isaiah sees the LORD punish "the army of heaven in heaven and the kings of the earth on earth" (Isaiah 24:21, fresh rendering), and the fall of the shining star, son of the dawn (Isaiah 14:12–15). Rashi and Midrash Tehillim, citing Isaiah 24:21, explain "the princes" as the heavenly princes. Others take it of human rulers who fall in battle or lose their thrones.

a: for you will take all the nations as your own
p: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 gave the nations to the sons of God and kept Israel for the LORD. Now God claims them all.
b: Tinchal is "you will take as your inheritance", the language of Deuteronomy 32:8–9, where the nations received their inheritance under the sons of God while "the LORD's own share is his people". The prayer asks God to end that arrangement and rule every nation directly. Christian readers hear the same hope in Revelation: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ" (Revelation 11:15). The psalm ends with the worshipers, who have just overheard the trial, asking God to carry out the sentence.

a: Stand up, God! Be the judge of the earth
p: In Orthodox churches this verse is sung on Holy Saturday as the priest scatters leaves, announcing Christ's victory.
b: In the Byzantine liturgy of Holy Saturday, after the readings, the choir sings "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations" (the Greek of this verse) again and again, while the priest scatters bay leaves through the church. It is sung at the point where the mood turns from mourning to the first news of the resurrection: Christ, having gone down among the dead, rises to judge and to claim the nations. Jewish worshipers end the Tuesday psalm with the same plea, for God to set right the world's courts.

a: A song. A psalm of Asaph.
p: Psalm 83 closes both the Asaph group (73–83) and the Elohistic Psalter (42–83).
b: This is the last psalm under Asaph's name, and the last of the run of psalms that prefer "God" to "the LORD" (see 82:1). It is also the only Asaph psalm that is purely a community's cry for help against a coalition of enemies. Fittingly, it ends with the divine name itself: "you whose name is the LORD" (83:18).

a: God, give yourself no rest!
p: Domi means stillness or silence. Isaiah uses it for watchmen who give God no rest until he acts.
b: Literally "God, let there be no silence for you". Domi is rest or stillness. Isaiah's watchmen are told "take no rest, and give him no rest" until he makes Jerusalem renowned (Isaiah 62:6–7, the same word). Three verbs pile up here (silent, mute, still), because God's silence is the worshipers' problem. The Greek read domi as "likeness" (from damah, "be like") and rendered it "God, who will be likened to you?"; the rest of the verse matches the Hebrew (see the variant).

a: the ones you shelter
p: Tsefunekha means "your hidden, treasured ones", the people God hides in his shelter.
b: From tsafan, "hide, store up, treasure". God hides his people in the shelter of his presence (31:20) and in his booth on the day of trouble (27:5). The enemies plot against people God is keeping safe. The Greek renders "your holy ones"; Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew, "your secret".

a: Come, we will wipe them out so they are no nation
t: A verse read in every generation
p: Jews have heard this verse in each persecution. Some Christians read it as a prophecy of a modern war.
b: The plotters want Israel's very name forgotten. The Passover Haggadah says that "in every generation they rise against us to destroy us", and Jewish readers have heard this verse in that light, from Haman to the twentieth century. In recent decades some Christian writers, especially among dispensationalists, have read Psalm 83 as a prophecy of a coming war between modern Israel and its Arab neighbors (the "Psalm 83 war", popularized by Bill Salus in 2008). Most scholars, Jewish and Christian, read the list as a poetic gathering of ancient enemies, and caution against mapping it onto modern nations.

a: they are making a pact against you
p: Berit is "covenant". The nations' treaty is aimed not only at Israel but at God.
b: The word for their alliance is berit, the same word as God's covenant with Israel. Plotting against God's people is treated as treaty-making against God himself. Compare Psalm 2, where the kings of the earth plot against the LORD and his anointed together (2:2).

a: Edom's tents and the Ishmaelites
p: Edom, desert tribes, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre and Assyria: every border at once. No known war matches.
b: The list circles Israel: Edom and Amalek to the south, the Ishmaelite and Hagrite tribes of the eastern desert, Moab and Ammon across the Jordan, Philistia on the coast, Tyre and Gebal to the north, and Assyria beyond. The Hagrites were desert tribes east of Gilead (1 Chronicles 5:10). Ten names suggest a complete set. No single historical alliance included all of them, so many scholars read the list as a poetic picture of total encirclement. Dates proposed range from Jehoshaphat's war (2 Chronicles 20) to the Assyrian period and even the Maccabean age, when similar neighbors attacked (1 Maccabees 5).

a: Gebal
p: Gebal may be Byblos, the Phoenician port, or a mountain region near Petra in Edom.
b: Gebal is the Hebrew name of Byblos on the Lebanese coast (Ezekiel 27:9), which would sit well beside Tyre. But it is listed between Edom's neighbors, and a region called Gebalene (Jibal) lay in the hills of Edom near Petra, so many scholars think that is meant. The Targum says "the Byblians".

a: Even Assyria is linked with them
p: Assyria as a mere helper of Moab and Ammon is odd for the great empire. It may be an early date, or a desert tribe.
b: Assyria appears only as "an arm" for Lot's descendants, Moab and Ammon (Genesis 19:36–38). The great Assyrian empire never played such a minor part. Some date the psalm to before Assyria's rise to empire or to its local alliances in the ninth and eighth centuries; others think of Asshurim, a desert tribe descended from Abraham (Genesis 25:3); others see Assyria as a stock name for any power in the north, as later Jewish writers used it for Persia or the Seleucids. The Targum names Sennacherib.

a: Treat them like Midian
p: The psalm asks God to repeat the wins of Deborah and Gideon (Judges 4–8).
b: Two stories from Judges are recalled. Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera, commander of Jabin, king of Hazor, at "the Kishon River" (Judges 4:7, 13; 5:21). Gideon routed Midian with three hundred men (Judges 7). These became Israel's pattern for impossible rescues: Isaiah speaks of breaking the oppressor's rod "as on the day of Midian" (Isaiah 9:4). In the story Jabin was not killed at the Kishon; the psalm compresses the two victories into one prayer.

a: who were wiped out at Endor
p: Endor lay south of Mount Tabor. Judges does not name it, so the psalm may know a fuller local story.
b: En-dor was a town near Mount Tabor and the Hill of Moreh, assigned to Manasseh (Joshua 17:11). Both Barak's battle (from Tabor, Judges 4:6–14) and Gideon's (near Moreh, Judges 7:1) were fought in this area, so the town could belong to either story, though Judges names it for neither. It is better known as the home of the woman Saul consulted (1 Samuel 28:7). "Manure on the soil" is a curse picture: unburied bodies left to rot (Jeremiah 8:2).

a: Oreb and Zeeb
p: Oreb and Zeeb, Midian's commanders, mean "Raven" and "Wolf". Gideon killed them and kings Zebah and Zalmunna.
b: Judges tells it: "They killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the Winepress of Zeeb" (Judges 7:25). The names mean Raven and Wolf. Zebah and Zalmunna, Midian's kings, were killed by Gideon himself (Judges 8:21). The psalm asks that today's noblemen meet the same end. Isaiah recalls "the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb" (Isaiah 10:26).

a: Let God's grazing lands
p: The enemies want God's own land. Jehoshaphat's prayer uses the same idea when Moab and Ammon invade.
b: Ne'ot are pastures, here the land of Israel as God's own grazing country (compare 23:2; Jeremiah 23:10). The complaint matches King Jehoshaphat's prayer when Moab, Ammon and Mount Seir invaded: "They are coming to drive us out of your property, the land you gave us to take possession of" (2 Chronicles 20:11). In that story a Levite "one of Asaph's sons" prophesied victory (2 Chronicles 20:14), and the Korahites sang (2 Chronicles 20:19). Many commentators since Delitzsch have suggested that Psalm 83 belongs to that crisis; others think the parallel is one of theme, not date.

a: set them whirling like a thistle wheel
p: Galgal is a wheel, and the dry seed head of a desert thistle that rolls before the wind.
b: Galgal means "wheel" (so the Greek and Latin, "like a wheel"). Isaiah uses it in the same picture: nations chased "like whirling dust before a storm" (Isaiah 17:13). Travelers in the Holy Land have long described the wild artichoke (Gundelia), whose dried globe breaks off in autumn and bowls across the fields in the wind. "Straw" (qash) is the stubble left after harvest.

a: so they will search for your name, LORD
t: Curse with a door left open
p: The psalm asks for shame so that enemies will seek God, but also for their end. Traditions pray it in different ways.
b: The prayer is fierce: storm, fire, shame, ruin. Yet verse 16 hopes the enemies will "search for your name", and verse 18 that they will "learn" who the LORD is. Some readers take that as hope for the nations' conversion; others say verse 17 shows the knowledge comes too late, as Pharaoh learned the LORD's name only in defeat (Exodus 14:4, 18). Jewish worship has kept the psalm among Israel's prayers in times of danger. The Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves it out (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131; see the card on the chapter page), and many Christians pray it as a prayer against evil itself, while others hold that such curses belong to the old covenant and are answered by Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).

a: you whose name is the LORD
p: The psalm ends on God's name. The KJV printed "JEHOVAH" here, and Jehovah's Witnesses often cite the verse.
b: After a whole psalm of "God" (see 82:1), the name YHWH appears at the climax: the nations must learn that the LORD alone is Most High. The KJV spells the name out here, "whose name alone is JEHOVAH", one of only four places where it prints the name standing alone (with Exodus 6:3; Isaiah 12:2; Isaiah 26:4). Jehovah's Witnesses use the verse to stress using God's name; most Jewish and Christian traditions say "the LORD" (Adonai), following Jewish reverence for the name. "Jehovah" itself is a hybrid, the consonants YHWH read with the vowels of Adonai.

a: Of the sons of Korah
p: Korah's descendants survived his rebellion and became Temple singers and gatekeepers. Eleven psalms carry their name.
b: Korah led a revolt against Moses and died in it, "But the sons of Korah did not die" (Numbers 26:11). Chronicles lists Korahites as guards of the thresholds and as singers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19). Psalms 42–49 form the first Korah collection; Psalms 84–85 and 87–88 a second, which opens Book III's last section after the Asaph psalms. Love for Zion and its Temple runs through them all (46; 48; 84; 87).

a: How dearly loved are your dwellings
p: Yedidot means "beloved", from the same root as Jedidiah, Solomon's other name. It is a lover's word.
b: Yedidot comes from yadid, "beloved", the root of Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD", the name Nathan gave Solomon (2 Samuel 12:25). The Temple is not merely lovely to look at; it is loved, the way a person is loved. "Dwellings" (mishkenot) is plural, perhaps for the several courts and buildings, perhaps as a plural of majesty. The word is related to mishkan, the tabernacle. Brahms set verses 1, 2 and 4 as the gentle fourth movement of his German Requiem (1868).

a: The little bird, too, has found a house
p: Small birds nest in the Temple's walls, close to God all year. The pilgrim envies them.
b: Tsippor is any small bird; deror is probably the swallow or swift, which nests in walls and eaves. Birds nesting in temple buildings were a familiar sight in the ancient world. Herodotus tells of a man who removed sparrows' nests from Apollo's temple at Branchidae and was rebuked by the god for driving out his "suppliants" (Herodotus 1.159). The pilgrim, who can come only at festivals, envies the birds that live there. Some readers take the birds as a figure for the pilgrim himself, finally at home.

a: your altars, LORD of Armies
p: Birds could not nest on a burning altar. The line may mean "near your altars", or be the pilgrim's cry.
b: The Hebrew says the bird sets her chicks "et your altars", which can mean "beside". Ibn Ezra reports a medieval dispute: one teacher said even the birds know the holy place and come near the altar; another mocked the idea that birds have such knowledge, and read the line as the pilgrim's own longing, "the bird has found a home, but I have not found your altars". Many modern readers take "Your altars!" as an exclamation: that is what the psalmist's heart is set on.

a: Happy are the ones who live in your house
p: This line, with 144:15 and Psalm 145, is the Ashrei, said three times daily in the synagogue.
b: In Hebrew Bibles this is 84:5, Ashrei yoshvei veitekha. The Jewish prayer book places it, with 144:15, before Psalm 145, and the whole unit, called the Ashrei, is said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon. The Talmud says that whoever says Psalm 145 three times a day is assured of the world to come (Bavli Berakhot 4b). "Those who live in your house" were first the priests and Levites; in the prayer book they become everyone who sits in the synagogue to pray.

a: who carries the highways in the heart
p: Mesillot are built-up roads, here the pilgrim roads to Jerusalem. The Greek has "ascents".
b: Literally "highways (are) in their hearts". Mesillah is a raised road, like the highway Isaiah sees prepared for God's people (Isaiah 40:3; 62:10). The pilgrim's heart is already on the road to Zion. The Greek reads "ascents in his heart", echoing the "Songs of Ascents" (120–134). Some scholars emend to "in whose heart are your ways"; the Targum reads "trust in their hearts". The change from "anyone" (singular) to "their" is in the Hebrew; the Plain smooths it.

a: the Valley of Baca
t: Valley of balsam, or of weeping?
p: Baca is a tree, the baka of 2 Samuel 5:23. The Greek and Latin heard bakhah "weep": the valley of tears.
b: Bakha is the name of a tree, perhaps the balsam or a kind of poplar that grows in dry places; David's army waited by "the baka trees" in 2 Samuel 5:23–24. A valley of such trees would be dry ground on the way to Jerusalem. The Greek, the Latin and the Targum connect it with bakhah, "weep": "the valley of weeping" (vallis lacrimarum). From that came the Christian phrase "vale of tears" for this life, used in the prayer Salve Regina. No place of that name is known, so it may be a poetic name.

a: wraps it in blessings
p: Berakhot "blessings" and berekhot "pools" have the same letters. Moreh means early rain, and also "teacher".
b: The vowels in the traditional text give berakhot, "blessings". With different vowels the same letters read berekhot, "pools", which suits the springs in the line before; the KJV has "pools". Moreh is the early autumn rain (Joel 2:23), but the same word means "teacher". The Greek took it so: "the lawgiver will give blessings" (see the variant), and Rashi, too, speaks of the Teacher. At Qumran the community's leader was called moreh ha-tsedeq, "the Teacher of Righteousness", a title some think drew on this double sense in Joel 2:23.

a: They walk on, from strength to strength
p: Normally travelers tire. These pilgrims gain strength as they near Zion.
b: Chayil is strength, ability, even an army. Ordinary travelers grow weary on a long road; these pilgrims grow stronger the nearer they come. Isaiah says those who wait for the LORD "will run and not be weary" (Isaiah 40:31, fresh rendering). Some take "from strength to strength" as from one fortified town to the next along the road. Jewish custom draws on the phrase: one who leaves the synagogue goes to the house of study, "from strength to strength" (Bavli Berakhot 64a).

a: the one who is our shield
p: "Our shield" parallels "your anointed", so it is probably the king. Later readers saw the high priest or the Messiah.
b: The two halves of the verse match: "our shield" and "your anointed". The king was called the people's shield (89:18; 47:9), and "the LORD's anointed" is his title (1 Samuel 24:6). So this is a prayer for the king, which suggests the psalm was sung while Judah still had kings. After the exile, readers applied it to the anointed high priest, and later to the coming Messiah. The Targum makes it "the merit of our fathers" and "your Messiah". Others take "our shield" as God himself, called "shield" in verse 11.

a: I choose to stand at the threshold of my God's house
p: The verb is found only here. The KJV's "doorkeeper" fits the Korahites, who guarded the thresholds.
b: Histofef appears nowhere else; it comes from saf, "threshold", and means to stand or sit at the doorway. The KJV's famous "I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God" is a fair guess, and fits a Korahite singer, for the sons of Korah served "as guards of the tent's thresholds" (1 Chronicles 9:19). The line also has an odd word order: "better a day in your courts than a thousand I have chosen". The Targum explains the thousand as "a thousand in exile". Rashi says one day there and then death is better than a thousand years elsewhere.

a: The LORD God is sun and shield
p: Only here is God called a sun outright. The Targum and the Greek both avoided the image.
b: Nowhere else does the Bible say directly that God is a sun (shemesh), though it comes close: "the sun of righteousness" will rise (Malachi 4:2), and God is light (27:1). In the ancient Near East the sun-god Shamash was the judge who sees everything, and Egyptian kings were called the sun. Israel's teachers were wary of sun worship (Deuteronomy 4:19; 2 Kings 23:11), and the versions show it. The Targum renders "like a high wall and a strong shield", and the Greek has "the Lord loves mercy and truth" (see the variant). Christian writers read the line of Christ, the light of the world.

a: happy is anyone who puts trust in you
t: A verse for the end of Sabbath
p: Jews say this verse at Havdalah, the ceremony that closes the Sabbath, and in daily prayers.
b: The last line, "LORD of Armies, happy is anyone who trusts in you", is one of the verses recited at Havdalah on Saturday night, as the Sabbath ends and the working week begins, with 46:7 and 20:9. It is also said in the daily service. The psalm's three "happy" sayings (verses 4, 5 and 12) move from those who live in God's house, to those on the road toward it, to anyone at all who trusts him, wherever they are.

a: you turned Jacob's fortunes back
t: "Restore the fortunes" or "bring back the captivity"
p: Shav shevut is an idiom for a full reversal. The old versions read it as bringing back captives.
b: The phrase shav shevut plays on two similar roots: shuv, "turn back", and shevut or shevit, which the ancient versions took from shavah, "take captive". So the Greek, the Latin, the Targum and the KJV read "you brought back the captivity of Jacob". Most scholars today read it as an idiom for a complete turn of fortune, used even where no exile is in view (Job 42:10). Here both senses fit, since many date the psalm after the return from Babylon. The written text (shevit) and the spoken text (shevut) differ by one letter (see the variant).

a: You carried off the guilt of your people
p: Nasa 'avon, "lift guilt", is the phrase of God's self-description in Exodus 34:7.
b: To "lift" or "carry" guilt is the Hebrew idiom for forgiving: the burden is taken away. God names himself as one "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (Exodus 34:7), using the same verb. "Put a cover over" (kissah) is another picture of forgiveness (32:1). The past tense ("you carried off", "you covered") recalls an earlier mercy, which becomes the ground for the prayer in verse 4.

a: Turn us around, God of our rescue
p: Shuv "turn" runs through the psalm: God turned, will he turn again, and turn us?
b: The verb shuv is the psalm's hinge. God "turned" Jacob's fortunes (verse 1) and "turned back" from anger (verse 3); now the people ask, "Turn us" (verse 4) and "Is it not you who will turn?" (verse 6), and the answer warns them not to "turn back" to foolishness (verse 8). The same word means "repent". Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew renders "God of our rescue" as Deus Iesus noster, "God our Jesus", because the name Jesus (Yeshua) comes from the same root as yesha', "rescue".

a: bring us back to life
p: Many scholars think the people had come back from exile but found hard times. Haggai describes such a time.
b: The psalm remembers a past mercy (verses 1–3) and asks for a new one (verses 4–7). A common reading sets it after some exiles returned from Babylon in 538 BC: they were home, but crops failed and the Temple lay unfinished. Haggai says the sky held back its dew and the earth its produce (Haggai 1:10–11), which suits the promise that "our land will give its crops" (85:12). Others date it before the exile, to a drought or a defeat, and read verses 1–3 as a prophetic perfect.

a: I will listen for what God, the LORD, says
p: A single voice, perhaps a Temple prophet, waits for God's reply and then gives it.
b: The "I" changes the psalm. After the people's prayer, someone listens, and what follows (verses 8–13) is God's answer of peace. Mowinckel and others think a Levite or prophet spoke such answers in the Temple service, as Jahaziel did in 2 Chronicles 20:14–17; Habakkuk too stands at his post to see what God will say (Habakkuk 2:1). "Peace" (shalom) means wholeness, not just the end of war. The warning at the end shows that the promise is not automatic.

a: so that glory will make its home in our land
p: Shakhan "dwell" gives the word Shekhinah. Ezekiel saw the glory leave the Temple and come back.
b: Lishkon kavod, "for glory to dwell". From shakhan came the rabbinic word Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence. Ezekiel watched God's glory leave the Temple before its fall and saw it return in a vision (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 43:2–5). The psalm hopes for that return in the land itself. John uses the matching Greek verb for the Word who "pitched his tent among us. We gazed at his glory" (John 1:14).

a: Loyal love and faithfulness have met
p: The rabbis made these four into a debate in heaven over creating humans. Bernard made them a Christmas story.
b: Hesed, faithfulness (emet, also "truth"), righteousness and peace appear as persons who meet and kiss. Genesis Rabbah (8:5) tells that when God was about to create the human being, Loyal Love said "Create him", Truth said "Do not", Righteousness said "Create", and Peace said "Do not", and God cast Truth to the earth, citing 85:11. Bernard of Clairvaux (1100s) turned it into a Christian parable of four sisters at odds over fallen humanity, reconciled when Christ is born. That story, the "Four Daughters of God", was retold in medieval plays. The Book of Common Prayer appoints Psalm 85 for Christmas Day.

a: Faithfulness sprouts out of the earth
p: Earth and heaven join: faithfulness grows up, righteousness looks down. Christian writers read Christ's birth here.
b: The picture is of a harvest: faithfulness springs up like a plant (tsamach), while righteousness leans out of heaven like someone at a window (nishqaf). Earth and heaven answer each other, and the next verse makes it literal with rain and crops. Augustine, preaching at Christmas (Sermon 185), said: "Truth has sprung from the earth: Christ is born of a woman", and the Latin Veritas de terra orta est became a Christmas text. The word tsemach, "sprout", was also a title for the coming king (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8).

a: A prayer of David.
t: A prayer made of other prayers
p: The only David psalm in Book III, built almost entirely from phrases found elsewhere in Scripture.
b: Book III has only this one psalm with David's name. Almost every line has a twin elsewhere: the poor and needy speaker of verse 1 (compare 40:17), the lifted soul of verse 4 (25:1), the request to be taught God's way in verse 11 (27:11), the arrogant who seek the speaker's life in verse 14 (54:3), the gods who are not like the LORD in verse 8 (Exodus 15:11), and the great confession of Exodus 34:6 in verse 15. Scholars call it an anthology psalm. Rather than proving it late or unoriginal, the borrowing shows how Israel prayed: with words already tested by others.

a: I am one of your loyal ones
p: Chasid means a person bound to God by hesed. It is a claim of belonging, not of perfection.
b: Chasid comes from hesed, "loyal love". It names someone inside the covenant bond: loyal to God and loved by him. It is not a boast of sinlessness, and verse 5 asks for pardon. Later the word came to mean a pious person, and it names the Hasidim, both the pious Jews of the Maccabean age and the movement founded in the 1700s. The Greek translates hosios, "holy".

a: Show me grace, Lord
p: Adonai "Lord" appears seven times here (verses 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 15), along with the name YHWH four times.
b: This is Adonai, "my Lord, Master", not the name YHWH, so the Plain prints "Lord" in small letters and "LORD" for the name, as everywhere on this site. A servant speaks to his master; he calls himself "your servant" three times (verses 2, 4, 16). Adonai appears seven times.

a: among the gods not one is like you
t: None like you among the gods
p: The line comes from the Song of the Sea. Jews sing it when the Torah scroll is taken out.
b: The source is Moses' song: "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11). The psalm speaks of "gods" without fear (compare 82:1), but always to say that the LORD is beyond them all, and verse 10 ends, "You are God, you alone". In the synagogue, the service for taking out the Torah scroll opens with this verse in Hebrew, Ein kamokha va'elohim Adonai.

a: Every nation that you made will come
p: The victors in Revelation sing that all nations will come and worship, echoing this verse.
b: Those who have overcome the beast sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: "All nations will come and worship in front of you, because your acts of justice have been made known" (Revelation 15:4). The hope that the nations God made will one day bow to him runs through the Prophets (Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 66:23; Zechariah 14:16). In the middle of a personal plea for help, the psalmist sets his trouble inside that world-wide hope.

a: Make my heart one
p: Yached levavi asks God to unite the heart. The Greek heard a different verb: "let my heart rejoice".
b: Yached means "make one", from echad, "one": gather my scattered loyalties into one. Jeremiah's promise is the same: "I will give them one heart and one way" (Jeremiah 32:39, fresh rendering), as is the warning against the double-minded in James 4:8. The Greek and the Gallican Latin read yichad, from chadah, "rejoice": "let my heart rejoice to fear your name" (see the variant). Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew has unicum fac cor meum, "make my heart single".

a: the lowest Sheol
p: She'ol tachtiyyah is the deepest part of the world of the dead. He means he was close to death.
b: "The lowest Sheol" (She'ol tachtiyyah) appears in the Song of Moses, where God's anger "burns to the bottom of Sheol" (Deuteronomy 32:22). The psalmist is not saying he had died, but that he had come to the very edge. The past tense may be thanks for an earlier rescue, or confidence that God will rescue. The Latin ex inferno inferiori led some medieval writers to speak of levels of hell.

a: But you, Lord, are a God compassionate and gracious
p: Verse 15 repeats God's own words to Moses in Exodus 34:6, Israel's most quoted statement about God.
b: When God passed by Moses on Sinai he called out, "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). That confession is echoed throughout the Bible (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8). The Plain here uses the same English as the site's Exodus, since the Hebrew is the same. The psalmist sets it against the arrogant of verse 14: they ignore God, but God is not like them.
r: Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8

a: your servant girl's son
p: A slave born in the house belonged to the family from birth. The psalmist says he is God's by birth.
b: Ben-amatekha, "son of your female servant", meant a slave born in the household, who had never known another master (Exodus 23:12; compare Psalm 116:16). The psalmist claims a lifelong belonging. Christian readers, starting with Augustine, heard Christ speaking, the son of Mary, who called herself "the Lord's servant" (Luke 1:38). The Plain uses "servant" for 'eved throughout this part; the word can also mean "slave".

a: What he founded stands on the holy mountains
p: Literally "his foundation in the holy mountains". The psalm starts mid-thought, and the text may be damaged.
b: The Hebrew is very compressed: "His foundation on the holy mountains". "His" is God, and his foundation is Zion, named in the next verse. "Mountains" is plural, for the hills of Jerusalem. Psalm 87 is short, choppy and hard throughout, and many scholars think lines have been lost or moved; some rearrange the verses. The Plain follows the order of the Hebrew and marks the hardest places in notes.

a: The gates of Zion
p: The gates stand for the city itself, where courts met and people came and went.
b: The gate was the city's public square: there elders judged, business was done and news was told (Ruth 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 25:7). To love Zion's gates is to love the city and the life within it. Radak says gates are named because the elders and the wise sit there. The Targum turns them into the gates of the houses of study, loved above all the synagogues of Jacob.

a: Splendid things are being said of you
p: Augustine took "city of God" from this verse for his great book, and John Newton made it a hymn.
b: Augustine opened Book 11 of The City of God by quoting this verse, with 48:1–2 and 46:4–5: Scripture itself calls the heavenly city "the city of God". John Newton, the former slave trader turned pastor, wrote "Glorious things of thee are spoken, Zion, city of our God" (1779), now sung to Haydn's tune Austria. Jewish readers kept the earthly city in view: the Talmud and the Midrash speak of the honor of Jerusalem, and the Targum adds "forever". What the "splendid things" are, the next verses say.

a: I will call Rahab and Babylon to mind
p: This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho. It is the sea monster's name, used for Egypt.
b: Two different Hebrew names are spelled "Rahab" in English. The woman of Jericho is Rachav (Joshua 2:1). This is Rahav, "arrogance", the name of a sea monster God crushed (89:10; Job 26:12; Isaiah 51:9), used as a nickname for Egypt: "Rahab who sits still" (Isaiah 30:7). So the list names the great powers: Egypt and Babylon, the empires to the south and east, Philistia and Tyre nearby, and distant Cush (Sudan).

a: as ones who know me
p: The nations that oppressed Israel are named as people who know God and were born in Zion.
b: "Know me" is covenant language: Jeremiah promises that all Israel will know the LORD (Jeremiah 31:34). Here it is said of Egypt and Babylon, the empires of Israel's slavery and exile. The verse echoes the promise that "Egypt my people" and "Assyria my handiwork" will stand beside Israel (Isaiah 19:24–25). Readers differ on the meaning. Many take it as the conversion of the nations. Rashi reads it of Jews born abroad, whom the nations will bring home as a gift. The Targum makes the kings born there David and Solomon. Christian readers saw the Church gathered from every nation.

a: One after another was born in her
p: The Greek read "Mother Zion". Paul calls the Jerusalem above "our mother".
b: Literally "a man and a man was born in her": person after person. The Greek has "'Mother Zion,' a man will say" (see the variant), and that reading shaped Christian prayer. Isaiah pictures Zion giving birth to a nation in one day (Isaiah 66:7–8). Paul writes: "the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother" (Galatians 4:26, fresh rendering), and Hebrews speaks of "the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" and the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven (Hebrews 12:22–23).

a: when he writes the peoples down
p: God keeps a city roll and enters foreigners as native-born. It is a picture behind the "book of life".
b: Cities kept registers of citizens, and returning exiles were listed by family (Ezra 2; Nehemiah 7). Isaiah speaks of "everyone recorded for life in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 4:3, fresh rendering), and Ezekiel of false prophets left out of "the register of the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 13:9). Here God writes the foreign peoples into the roll as if they had been born in Zion. Revelation's "book of life" continues the image: only "those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life" enter the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:27). The Talmud reads the verse before, 87:5, of those born in Zion and of those who long to see it (Bavli Ketubot 75a).

a: Both singers and pipers
t: A line nobody is sure of
p: Cholelim may be pipers or dancers, and the sentence has no verb. The versions all differ.
b: The Hebrew reads "and singers like cholelim: all my springs in you". Cholelim may come from chalil, "flute" (so "pipers"), or from chul, "whirl, dance" (Rashi links it to the dances of Judges 21:21). There is no verb, and it is not clear who speaks. The Greek reads quite differently (see the variant). The likeliest sense is a festival procession singing Zion's praise, but the line is uncertain.

a: Every spring of mine is in you
p: Springs are the sources of life. The prophets saw a river flowing from the Temple.
b: A ma'yan is a spring, a source. The singers say that everything that gives them life comes from Zion. Jerusalem had one real spring, the Gihon, but the prophets saw more: a river whose streams gladden the city of God (46:4), water flowing from the Temple to heal the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:1–12), a fountain from the LORD's house (Joel 3:18). Jesus speaks of rivers of living water (John 7:37–38), and Revelation of the river of life from the throne (Revelation 22:1). Midrash Tehillim says Israel sings a new song every hour, like a spring that flows fresh.

a: On mahalath leannoth
p: Probably a tune or musical direction. Machalat may mean "sickness", and le'annot "to sing" or "to afflict".
b: Machalat also heads Psalm 53. It may be a tune name, or a word from chalah, "be sick", or from machol, "dance". Le'annot can mean "for singing" (from 'anah II), "for answering" (so the Greek, "for answering"), or "for afflicting" (from 'anah III). The KJV simply copied the Hebrew, as the Plain does. Rashi gives a reading that fits the psalm: it concerns one "sick with love and afflicted", the people of Israel in the pains of exile.

a: A maskil of Heman the Ezrahite
t: Heman, a wise man and a singer
p: Heman is named among the sages Solomon outdid, and among David's chief singers. The title joins him to Korah.
b: Solomon "was wiser than any human being: than Ethan the Ezrahite, than Heman and Calcol and Darda" (1 Kings 4:31). Chronicles lists Heman among the sons of Zerah of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:6) and also as a Levite, "Heman the singer", descended from Korah, one of David's three music leaders (1 Chronicles 6:33; 15:17, 19; 25:5). "Ezrahite" probably means "of Zerah's clan", though some read "native". The title is double, giving both the Korah group and Heman, perhaps because the psalm came into the Korah collection from a separate source. Psalm 89 is credited to the other Ezrahite, Ethan.

a: LORD, God of my rescue
t: The only light in the psalm
p: Psalm 88 never turns to praise. Its one hope is that the speaker still calls God "my rescue" and keeps praying.
b: Most laments end with trust or thanks. Psalm 88 does not; it ends in darkness (88:18). Yet it begins by calling the LORD "God of my rescue" and is addressed to him throughout. The speaker prays by day and night (verse 1), every day (verse 9) and in the morning (verse 13). Walter Brueggemann calls it a psalm of disorientation, and says its value is that it keeps speaking to God when nothing has changed. Many sufferers have found it the one psalm honest enough for them.

a: my life has touched Sheol
p: The psalm piles up names for the world of the dead: Sheol, the pit, the grave, Abaddon, the dark, forgetting.
b: Israel pictured the dead as going down to Sheol, a shadowy world under the earth. Psalm 88 uses nearly every word for it: Sheol (verse 3), the pit (bor, verses 4 and 6), the grave (qever, verses 5 and 11), Abaddon (verse 11), the dark (verses 6, 12 and 18), the deeps (verse 6), and the land of forgetting (verse 12). The dead are "shades" (verse 10). The speaker is alive but feels already counted among them (verse 4). See the gloss on Sheol at 86:13.

a: turned loose among the dead
p: Chofshi is the word for a freed slave. Ugaritic poems call the underworld "the house of freedom".
b: Chofshi means "free", as of a slave set free in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2). Among the dead it may mean freed from life's duties, as Rashi explains, "free from the world"; or cut loose and abandoned. King Uzziah lived with his skin disease in "a house set apart" (2 Kings 15:5), in Hebrew bet hachofshit, a "house of freedom". In the Ugaritic Baal poems the way into the underworld is through bt ḫpṯt, a "house of freedom" in the earth. So the word may name a place of seclusion for the sick or the dead. The Greek and Latin have simply "free among the dead".

a: who are cut off from your hand
p: The dead seem out of God's care. Other psalms say God is present even in Sheol.
b: The speaker says God no longer remembers the dead, and they are cut off from his hand, his care and power. Other texts say the same (6:5; 30:9; 115:17; Isaiah 38:18). But the Bible is not of one voice: "If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there" says 139:8, and Amos says not even Sheol can hide anyone from God (Amos 9:2). Scholars such as Philip Johnston note that Israel did not deny that God has power over the dead; it said the dead could no longer praise him in worship. Later Scripture speaks of God raising the dead (Daniel 12:2).

a: with all your breaking waves
p: Jonah uses the same words from inside the fish. Water is the Bible's picture of death and chaos.
b: Mishbarim are breakers, waves that crash. Jonah prays from the deep, "all your breakers and your waves passed over me" (Jonah 2:3), and the Korah psalm 42:7 has "all your breakers and your waves" too. Water and the deep stand for death and chaos (69:1–2; 18:4–5). Here, unusually, the waves are God's own: he is not rescuing the speaker from them; he is sending them. The verse ends with Selah, perhaps a pause.

a: You have put distance between me and those who know me
p: At the cross, Luke says, all who knew Jesus stood far off. His words echo the Greek of this verse.
b: The Greek of this verse reads "you have put my acquaintances far from me" (tous gnōstous mou). Luke says that at the crucifixion "All who knew him stood a long way off" (Luke 23:49), using the same word for acquaintances, an echo also of 38:11. Christian readers from the early church on have read Psalm 88 as the prayer of Christ in his passion and burial. The speaker is cut off twice: from God and from every friend (88:18).

a: I am locked in, and I will not get out
t: Sick, in prison, or in exile?
p: Shunned and shut in, the speaker may be gravely ill, perhaps with a skin disease that forced isolation.
b: Friends find the speaker "abhorrent" (to'evot), and he is "locked in". People with skin disease had to "live alone" outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46), and Uzziah lived in a house set apart (2 Kings 15:5). The words "from boyhood" (verse 15) suggest a lifelong illness. Others read a prison or a pit (compare Jeremiah 38:6). Jewish tradition read the whole psalm as Israel in exile, shut in among the nations. The text does not say which, and that has let readers in many kinds of trouble pray it.

a: Will the shades get up and give you thanks?
p: Refa'im are the dead in Sheol, and also a giant people of old. At Ugarit they were the royal dead.
b: Refa'im means the dead, weak shadows in Sheol (Isaiah 14:9; Isaiah 26:14; Proverbs 2:18; Job 26:5). The same word names an ancient people of great size (Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11), and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew renders "will giants rise?". In Ugaritic texts the rpum are dead kings and heroes, honored in rites for the royal dead. The Greek read rof'im, "physicians": "will physicians raise them up?" (see the variant). The Targum: "bodies that have dissolved in the dust".

a: Is it for the dead that you will do a wonder?
p: The questions assume the dead cannot praise God. Later Scripture answers them with the resurrection.
b: Each question in verses 10–12 expects the answer no: the dead do not see wonders or tell of God's love. The argument is a plea: rescue me now, while I can still praise you (compare 6:5; 30:9). Isaiah later says "your dead will live" and the shades will rise (Isaiah 26:19), and Daniel sees many who sleep in the dust awake (Daniel 12:2). Jon Levenson argues that the hope of resurrection grew from such prayers, from trust in God's power over death. Christian readers hear the questions answered on Easter: God did his greatest wonder for one who was dead.

a: or of your faithfulness in Abaddon
p: Abaddon, "destruction", is a name for the place of the dead. In Revelation it becomes the name of an angel.
b: Abaddon, from avad, "perish", stands beside Sheol and death in the wisdom books: "Sheol lies naked before him; / there is no cover over Abaddon" (Job 26:6; compare Job 28:22; Proverbs 15:11). In Revelation the abyss has a king: "His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon" (Revelation 9:11). Here it is simply the place where no one tells of God's faithfulness.

a: the land of forgetting
p: Erets neshiyyah: the dead forget, and are forgotten.
b: Neshiyyah is from nashah, "forget". The land of the dead is where the dead remember nothing and no one remembers them (31:12; Ecclesiastes 9:5). It echoes verse 5, where even God "no longer remembers" them. The Latin terra oblivionis gave Christian poets the phrase "land of oblivion".

a: in the morning my prayer is there to meet you
p: The speaker keeps praying, day and night and at dawn, though no answer comes.
b: The verb qiddem means to come early, to go out and meet. His prayer will be waiting for God at daybreak, the time when help was hoped for (46:5; 5:3). Midrash Tehillim says the angel in charge of prayers goes before them, and the Greek has "my prayer will come before you". The persistence is the point: the speaker cries in verses 1, 9 and 13, and each time the description of his misery grows.

a: Why keep your face hidden from me?
p: God's hidden face means his favor withdrawn. The lament psalms ask "why" and "how long".
b: To see God's face is to know his favor (the priestly blessing, Numbers 6:25–26); for God to hide it is abandonment (13:1; 27:9; Deuteronomy 31:17). The "why" (lamah) links this psalm with 22:1, the cry Jesus prayed from the cross (Mark 15:34). Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust wrote of hester panim, "the hiding of the face", as a way to speak of God's absence without denying God.

a: I am numb
p: Afunah appears only here. Guesses include "helpless", "distraught" and "numb". The Greek read "perplexed".
b: The word afunah is found nowhere else in the Bible, and its meaning is lost. The KJV has "I am distracted". Many scholars link it to a root meaning "be numb, turn back"; others emend to afugah, "I grow faint" (compare 77:2). Rashi took it from ofen: "your terror is set firm in my heart". The Greek has "having been lifted up, I was brought low and perplexed", and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew "I was troubled". The Plain's "numb" is a guess, offered as such.

a: my companions are the dark
p: The Hebrew ends with the noun machshakh, "darkness". No other psalm ends so bleakly.
b: The final words are meyudda'ai machshakh, "my acquaintances: darkness". The line can be read "my companions are the dark" (the Plain), "darkness is my companion", or "my acquaintances are in darkness" (the KJV's "mine acquaintance into darkness", supplying a verb from the first half). Every reading ends in the dark. The Targum has "to those who know me I am hidden in darkness". Lament psalms usually turn to trust at the end; this one never does, and the Psalter keeps it anyway, followed at once by a psalm that begins with loyal love (89:1).

a: A maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite.
p: Ethan is the second wise man of 1 Kings 4:31. The Talmud says he was Abraham.
b: Ethan stands first in the list of sages Solomon surpassed (1 Kings 4:31), next to Heman of Psalm 88, and Chronicles names an Ethan of Zerah's clan (1 Chronicles 2:6) and an Ethan among David's Levite singers (1 Chronicles 15:17, 19), perhaps the same as Jeduthun. The Talmud identifies Ethan the Ezrahite with Abraham, reading "Ezrahite" as "the one from the east" (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), and the Targum of verse 3 accordingly says God made a covenant "with Abraham my chosen". Ibn Ezra took Ethan as the son of Zerah, who foresaw the fall of David's kingdom.

a: The LORD's acts of loyal love I will sing forever
t: Hesed and faithfulness, seven times each
p: Hesed and emunah, "loyal love" and "faithfulness", each appear seven times. The lament turns them against God.
b: Chasdei is plural, "acts of loyal love". The psalm uses hesed seven times (verses 1, 2, 14, 24, 28, 33, 49) and emunah, "faithfulness", seven times (verses 1, 2, 5, 8, 24, 33, 49). Both words are the vocabulary of covenant: kindness that keeps its promises. They carry the hymn and the promise, and at the end the lament throws them back: "Where, Lord, are your first acts of loyal love?" (89:49). Mozart set the Latin of this verse, Misericordias Domini cantabo in aeternum, as an offertory (K. 222, 1775).
orig: חַסְדֵי יְהוָה עוֹלָם אָשִׁירָה (chasdei YHWH olam ashirah)

a: Loyal love will stand built forever
p: Olam chesed yibbaneh can also be read "a world built on loyal love". Jewish tradition loves the line.
b: Olam means "forever", but in later Hebrew it also means "world". Read that way, olam chesed yibbaneh says "the world will be built by loyal love". Midrash Tehillim has Ethan answer, when asked what the world stands on, "The world is built on loyal love." The sentence became a favorite Jewish saying and a popular song, a summons to build the world through acts of kindness. In the psalm the building is first the house of David (89:4), as 2 Samuel 7:11–13 promised that God would build a house for David.

a: I have made a covenant with the one I chose
p: 2 Samuel 7 never uses the word covenant or oath. Psalm 89, like 2 Samuel 23:5 and Psalm 132, does.
b: Nathan's message in 2 Samuel 7 is a promise; it does not say "covenant" (berit) or "swear". Psalm 89 calls it a covenant four times (verses 3, 28, 34, 39) and an oath three times (verses 3, 35, 49). David's last words already speak of "a covenant with me that lasts forever" (2 Samuel 23:5), and Psalm 132:11–12 has God swearing to David. Peter's sermon draws on that tradition: David knew "God had sworn with an oath to him" to set one of his descendants on his throne (Acts 2:30, fresh rendering).

a: I will make your offspring firm for all time
p: Verses 3–4 sum up 2 Samuel 7:12–16: offspring, throne and permanence.
b: God promised David, "I will raise up your offspring to come after you" and "Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:12, 16). The psalm uses the same key words: "offspring" (zera'), "make firm" (kun), "build" (banah) and "throne" (kisse'). Notice what is missing: the Temple. In 2 Samuel the promise turns on a pun (David may not build God a house; God will build David's house), but Psalm 89 never mentions a temple at all. The full oracle comes in verses 19–37; see the chapter page for the two texts side by side.

a: in the gathering of the holy ones
p: The "holy ones" and "sons of the gods" are God's heavenly court, as in Psalm 82.
b: Qedoshim, "holy ones", are heavenly beings (Job 5:1; Job 15:15; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 8:13). They meet in a "gathering" (qahal, verse 5) and an "inner council" (sod, verse 7), and they are "the sons of the gods" (verse 6). This is the same divine council as 82:1, but here it does not stand trial; it praises the LORD and confesses that none of its members compares with him.

a: the sons of the gods
p: Bene elim, "sons of gods", means heavenly beings. The Targum and Greek turned them into angels and "sons of God".
b: Bene elim also opens Psalm 29, where they are called to give glory to the LORD (29:1). "Sons of" here means members of a class, so "divine beings" is the sense. The Greek has "sons of God", and the Targum "the hosts of angels". The question "Who is like the LORD?" was a common name in Israel: Micaiah, "who is like Yah?", and Michael, "who is like God?"

a: the inner council of the holy ones
p: Sod means a council and the secrets shared in it. Prophets claimed to have stood in God's sod.
b: A sod is a close circle of advisers, and also what they discuss in private (25:14). Jeremiah denies that the false prophets "stood in the LORD's council" (Jeremiah 23:18, 22), and Amos says God does nothing without revealing his sod to his servants the prophets (Amos 3:7). The psalm says even the members of that inner council stand in awe of God.

a: who is as strong as you, LORD?
t: "Yah", and a rare word for strong
p: The second "LORD" here is the short name Yah. Chasin, "strong", is a rare word, more at home in Aramaic.
b: The Hebrew is mi-khamokha chasin Yah, "who is like you, strong one, Yah?" Yah is the short form of the divine name, heard in hallelu-yah (see 104:35) and in names like Elijah. The Plain renders it "LORD", as it does the full name. Chasin, "mighty", occurs only here in biblical Hebrew but is common in Aramaic.

a: You are master of the sea when it swells
p: At Ugarit Baal defeated Sea; in Babylon, Marduk defeated Tiamat. Israel's poets say the LORD rules the sea.
b: In the Ugaritic Baal poems the storm god fights Prince Sea (Yam), also called Judge River, and wins kingship by the victory. In the Babylonian epic Enuma Elish Marduk splits the sea monster Tiamat to make the world. The psalm uses similar pictures (the swelling sea, Rahab crushed, the scattering of enemies) but with a difference: the sea is not a rival god, only something the LORD masters. The Gospels tell of Jesus quieting the sea, and the disciples asking, "Who can this be? The wind and the sea both do what he says!" (Mark 4:41). The verdict: a shared image, reworked.

a: You crushed Rahab like one cut down in battle
p: Rahab is the sea monster of old, and a name for Egypt. The Targum explains: "Rahab, that is wicked Pharaoh".
b: Rahab ("arrogance") is the chaos monster God defeated (Job 9:13; Job 26:12; Isaiah 51:9) and a nickname for Egypt (87:4; Isaiah 30:7). So the verse can be heard of creation and of the exodus at once, as Isaiah 51:9–10 joins them: the arm that pierced the dragon dried up the sea for the redeemed to cross. The Targum makes it explicit: "Rahab, that is wicked Pharaoh". The "arm" of God here returns in verses 13 and 21, where it strengthens David.

a: North and south: you made them
p: Tsafon "north" is also Mount Zaphon, Baal's mountain. Tabor and Hermon were old holy peaks.
b: Tsafon is "north", but also the name of Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra in Syria), where Baal had his palace in the Ugaritic poems; Zion is called "the heights of Zaphon" in 48:2. Yamin is "right hand", hence "south" for someone facing east; a few scholars emend to Mount Amanus. Tabor and Hermon, too, were places of worship (Hosea 5:1; Judges 3:3 names "Mount Baal-hermon"), and 1 Enoch makes Hermon the mountain where the Watchers came down (1 Enoch 6:6). The psalm claims all these peaks as the LORD's creation, singing his name. The Greek read yammim, "seas".

a: Your throne rests on righteousness and justice
p: In Egypt, a king's throne stood on a base shaped like the sign for ma'at, justice.
b: Makhon kis'akha, "the base of your throne". The Egyptologist Hellmut Brunner pointed out that Egyptian thrones were drawn standing on a platform shaped like the hieroglyph for ma'at, right order and justice, so the king literally sat on justice. The same line returns in 97:2. Proverbs says a king's throne is made firm by righteousness (Proverbs 16:12; Proverbs 25:5). Loyal love and faithfulness go ahead as attendants before the king.

a: Happy the people who know the shout of worship!
p: Teru'ah is the shout or trumpet blast of worship. Jews recite this verse after sounding the shofar on Rosh Hashanah.
b: Teru'ah is a loud shout or a trumpet blast (Numbers 10:5–6; Numbers 23:21), and the first of the seventh month is a day of teru'ah (Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 29:1). Midrash Tehillim reads the verse of Israel, who know how to please God with the shofar, and in the Rosh Hashanah service it is said right after the shofar is blown. To "walk by the light of God's face" is to live in his favor (4:6; Numbers 6:25).

a: Our shield is the LORD's own
p: The Hebrew can mean "the LORD is our shield" or "our shield, the king, belongs to the LORD".
b: Ki la-YHWH maginnenu, veliqdosh Yisra'el malkenu. Most modern scholars read it as the hinge of the psalm: "our shield" and "our king" are the Davidic king (compare 84:9; 47:9), and he belongs to the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. That leads straight into the oracle about David in verse 19. The older reading, in the KJV and the Targum, takes the Hebrew le- as "is": "the LORD is our defense, and the Holy One of Israel is our king". "The Holy One of Israel" is Isaiah's favorite name for God.

a: Back then you spoke in a vision to your loyal ones
p: 2 Samuel 7:17 calls Nathan's message "this vision". The psalm introduces its retelling the same way.
b: "Nathan passed on to David all these words, the whole of this vision" (2 Samuel 7:17). The psalm's chazon, "vision", picks up that word, so the oracle that follows is presented as Nathan's message retold in poetry. Who are "your loyal ones"? Rashi says Nathan and Gad. Many Hebrew manuscripts have the singular, "your loyal one", meaning Nathan or David (see the variant). The Greek has "your sons".

a: I have laid help on a warrior
t: Help, or a crown, or a young hero?
p: 'Ezer means "help". Scholars have proposed "crown" or "a young man" to fit the line better.
b: "I have set help upon a warrior" is an odd phrase. Some scholars read nezer, "crown" (the word in 89:39), for 'ezer: "I have set a crown on a warrior". Others, comparing an Ugaritic word ǵzr, "young man, hero", read "I have set a young man above the warrior" or "I have made a youth a hero". The ancient versions all have "help", and the Plain keeps it: God's help rests on David, as Rashi says, "to help him always".

a: I have found David my servant
p: Paul's sermon at Antioch quotes this line, joined with 1 Samuel 13:14.
b: In Pisidian Antioch Paul tells Israel's story and says God testified about David: "I have found David son of Jesse, a man to suit my heart, who will carry out everything I want" (Acts 13:22). The quotation joins this verse with 1 Samuel 13:14 ("a man to suit his own heart") and perhaps Isaiah 44:28. The anointing recalls the day "Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him" (1 Samuel 16:13). For Paul the point is the next step: from David's offspring God brought Israel a savior, Jesus (Acts 13:23).

a: His hand I will place on the sea
p: The king shares God's rule over the sea. "Sea" and "River" were the paired names of the chaos god at Ugarit.
b: In the hymn, God masters the sea (verses 9–10). Now he sets the king's hand on the sea and the rivers. In the Ugaritic poems Baal's enemy is called "Prince Sea" and "Judge River", the same pair, so the image may be of the king sharing God's victory over chaos. It also has a map behind it: a realm from the Mediterranean to the Euphrates (72:8; Exodus 23:31; 1 Kings 4:21). Many scholars also note a royal ideal common in the ancient Near East, the king as the god's earthly agent. Here the king is clearly second: God gives, God sets.

a: You are my Father
p: Nathan's promise, "I will be a father to him", becomes the king's prayer, "You are my Father".
b: In 2 Samuel God says of David's offspring, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14). Here David himself calls God "my Father". Psalm 2 makes the king God's son on the day of his crowning (2:7). In the Hebrew Bible this sonship is adoption into a role, not a claim that the king is divine; Israel too is God's son (Exodus 4:22). The New Testament applies the father-son words to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5; Mark 1:11). Jews pray to God as Avinu, "our Father", above all in the High Holy Day prayer Avinu Malkenu.

a: I, for my part, will make him firstborn
p: Revelation calls Jesus "the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth", echoing this verse.
