b: A firstborn son held the first rank and a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17). God calls Israel "my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22); here the title goes to the king, first among the world's kings. Revelation names Jesus "the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth" (Revelation 1:5), drawing on verses 27 and 37 together. Colossians calls him "the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15, fresh rendering). Jewish readers applied the verse to the Messiah too: a midrash in Exodus Rabbah (19:7) says, "I will make him firstborn: this is the King Messiah". The Targum limits it: firstborn among the kings of Judah's house.
r: Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 21:17; Revelation 1:5; Colossians 1:15; Colossians 1:18; Romans 8:29

a: most high over the kings of the earth
p: 'Elyon is God's title in 82:6 and 83:18. Only here is it used of a human king.
b: 'Elyon, "Most High", is a title of God (82:6; 83:18; Genesis 14:18). Deuteronomy uses it of Israel, set high above the nations (Deuteronomy 26:19; Deuteronomy 28:1). Only here does a king receive it. The bold word fits the psalm's picture: as God is supreme in the heavenly council (verses 5–8), his king is supreme among earth's rulers. The Greek softens it to "high above".

a: If his sons turn their backs on my law
p: 2 Samuel 7:14 speaks of one son and a father's rod. The psalm speaks of all his sons and the whole law.
b: 2 Samuel says of David's son: "If he does wrong, I will correct him with a rod such as men use, with blows such as people give" (2 Samuel 7:14). Psalm 89 makes it plural, "his sons", the whole dynasty, and spells out the wrong in the language of the covenant law: law, rulings, rules, commands. That is the vocabulary of Deuteronomy, which wanted the king to keep a copy of the law and read it all his life (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Chronicles, by contrast, leaves the "if" out entirely (1 Chronicles 17:13). The psalm keeps the threat but, as verse 33 says, puts a limit on it.

a: Yet my loyal love I will not break off from him
p: 2 Samuel 7:15 says God's loyal love will not turn away from David's son as it did from Saul.
b: "But my loyal love will not turn away from him the way I took it from Saul" (2 Samuel 7:15). The psalm repeats the promise with a stronger verb: afir, "I will break off" (some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read asir, "I will remove", closer to 2 Samuel, as reported in BHS, not checked myself; see the variant). This is the center of the problem the psalm raises. If God may punish but not withdraw his love, then the disaster in verses 38–45 looks like the one thing God swore he would not do.

a: I have taken one oath by my own holiness
p: God swears by his holiness, that is, by himself. The oath form "if I lie" means "I will never lie".
b: Hebrew oaths often leave the curse unspoken: "if I lie to David..." means "I will surely not lie". God swears "by his holiness" in Amos 4:2 as well. Having no one greater to swear by, he swears by his own being, as Hebrews says of the oath to Abraham (Hebrews 6:13–18). "One time" (achat) means once for all: it will not need repeating.

a: the witness in the skies is faithful
p: The witness may be the moon, the rainbow, or God himself. Revelation calls Jesus "the faithful witness".
b: Who is the witness? (1) The moon itself, fixed in the sky as long as the throne lasts. (2) The rainbow, the sign of God's covenant set in the clouds (Genesis 9:13). (3) God, or his throne in heaven, as in Job's "my witness is in heaven" (Job 16:19). Jeremiah ties David's covenant to day and night in the same way (Jeremiah 33:20–21). Revelation names Jesus "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5; compare Revelation 3:14), with the firstborn of verse 27 in the same line, so John seems to have this psalm in mind.

a: Yet you yourself have cast aside and refused
p: "But you": the speaker turns God's promises into a charge. A Spanish sage, Ibn Ezra says, could not bear to hear it.
b: Ve'attah, "and you", marks the turn. After 37 verses of praise and promise, the psalm accuses God of rejecting the king, disowning the covenant and defiling the crown (verses 38–45). Ibn Ezra reports that a great and pious scholar in Spain would neither read this psalm nor listen to it, because the poet speaks so harshly against God. Ibn Ezra himself defended it: the speaker is quoting the enemies' taunts and still believes the Messiah will come. Modern readers often see the psalm as a model of faithful protest, holding God to his word, like Moses (Exodus 32:11–13), Job and Habakkuk.

a: you have profaned his crown down to the dirt
p: Nezer is a consecrated crown. "Profane" answers verse 34: God said he would not profane his covenant.
b: Nezer is the crown or diadem of a consecrated person: the high priest's holy diadem (Exodus 29:6) and the crown put on young King Joash (2 Kings 11:12). It comes from the root of "Nazirite", set apart. The verb "profane" (chillel) has already been used twice: if the sons "profane my rules" (verse 31), God said, "My covenant I will not profane" (verse 34). Now the poet charges God with profaning the crown. The Greek reads "his holiness" (hagiasma), the Gallican Latin "his sanctuary".

a: You have knocked holes in all his walls
p: Broken walls, plunder, defeat and a young king shamed. Most scholars think of Jerusalem's fall in 587 BC.
b: The lament describes a military disaster: walls breached, forts ruined, the king plundered, his throne thrown down, his youth cut short (verses 40–45). Proposals include: Shishak's invasion under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25–26); the death of Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29); and most often the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 BC, when the walls were broken down and the king blinded and taken away (2 Kings 25:4–10), or the exile ten years earlier of Jehoiachin, who was eighteen (2 Kings 24:8–12). Some scholars (Clifford) think the hymn and oracle are older and the lament was added for the new crisis; others (Veijola) date the whole to the exile.

a: the flint edge of his sword
p: Tsur is "rock" or "flint", used for a blade's sharp edge, as with flint knives.
b: Literally "the rock of his sword". Flint (tsur) made the oldest knives (Exodus 4:25; Joshua 5:2), so the word came to mean a sharp edge. God "bends back" the blade so it is useless. The Greek has "the help of his sword", and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew "the strength of his sword".

a: You have stopped his brightness
p: Mittehoro, "from his brightness", is odd Hebrew. Many emend it to "his scepter from his hand".
b: The Hebrew hishbatta mittehoro reads "you made (him) stop from his purity/brightness". Tohar means "clarity, splendor" (Exodus 24:10) but more often ritual purity. The Greek has "you dissolved him from cleansing", and the Targum, "you abolished the priests who sprinkle on the altar and purify his people". Many scholars divide the letters differently, matteh hodo, "his glorious scepter", or matteh miyyado, "the scepter from his hand", which fits the throne in the next half line (see the variant).

a: You have made his youth short
p: "The days of his youth" fit Jehoiachin, exiled at eighteen. The Greek reads "the days of his throne".
b: Yemei 'alumav means "the days of his youth". If the king is a real person, Jehoiachin fits best: he became king at eighteen, reigned three months, and spent the rest of his youth a prisoner in Babylon (2 Kings 24:8, 12; 25:27–30). Others read "his youth" of the dynasty, cut off in its prime. Codex Vaticanus reads "the days of his throne", and other Greek manuscripts and the Gallican Latin "the days of his time" (see the variant).

a: Remember how short my lifetime is
p: The Hebrew reads "Remember, I, what lifespan". Many read "Remember, Lord". The versions all paraphrase.
b: Zekhor ani meh-chaled is awkward: "Remember, I, what (a) lifespan". A common emendation reads Adonai for ani: "Remember, Lord, what a lifespan is", as in verse 50. Cheled is the span of life (39:5). The Greek has "remember what my substance is", the Targum "remember that I was created from the dust", and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew "remember me from the depth". All agree on the sense: life is short, and if God does not act soon the speaker will not see it.

a: What man is there who lives on and never sees death
p: Every human dies, the king too. Christians answer with the one who saw death and was not held by it.
b: Gever is a strong man, even a hero, the word used of the warrior in verse 19. If even such a man must die, the king will die before God keeps his word. The Targum adds the angel of death. Peter's sermon at Pentecost argues from a related psalm that David died and was buried, but his descendant was not abandoned to the grave (Acts 2:24–31, citing Psalm 16:10). Hebrews says Christ died to free those held all their lives by fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

a: Where, Lord, are your first acts of loyal love
p: Isaiah 55:3 uses the same words, "David's acts of loyal love, made sure", and offers them to all the people.
b: The phrase chasadeikha harishonim ("your former acts of loyal love") echoes the psalm's opening (89:1) and Isaiah's promise: "I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful acts of loyal love promised to David" (Isaiah 55:3, fresh rendering). Isaiah uses the same two words, chasdei and ne'emanim, "made sure". Many scholars think Isaiah 55 answers Psalm 89 directly: the promise did not die with the monarchy, but passed to the whole people. Paul quotes Isaiah 55:3 in Acts 13:34 as fulfilled when God raised Jesus.

a: how I carry in my chest all the many peoples
p: The Hebrew is broken: "my bearing in my bosom all of many peoples". Most supply "the insults of".
b: Literally "my carrying in my bosom all many peoples". Most translators supply a word from the first line, "the insults of all the many peoples", or emend rabbim to rivei, "the quarrels of". The Targum has "I bore in my bosom all their blasphemies of many peoples"; Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew, "all the wrongs of the peoples". The Plain gives the Hebrew as it stands; the sense is clear from verse 51. "Your servants" is plural in the Leningrad Codex; many other Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac have the singular (see the variant).
orig: שְׂאֵתִי בְחֵיקִי כָּל־רַבִּים עַמִּים (se'eti vecheqi kol-rabbim 'ammim)

a: the insults they have thrown at the footprints of your anointed
p: 'Iqqevot are heels or footprints. The rabbis read "the footsteps of the Messiah": the last days before he comes.
b: 'Iqqevot meshichekha are the anointed king's heelprints: enemies mock wherever he walks. Jewish tradition read meshicha as the Messiah. The Targum renders "they have mocked the delay of the footsteps of your Messiah", and the Mishnah's famous phrase be'iqvot meshicha, "in the footsteps of the Messiah", describes the age of insolence and trouble just before he comes (Mishnah Sotah 9:15). Rashi explains the verse that way. So the psalm's last complaint became a hope: the mockery means his steps are near.

a: the insults your enemies have thrown, LORD
p: The Greek reads "the reproach... of your christ". Hebrews 11:26 speaks of Moses and "the reproach of Christ".
b: In the Greek, verses 50–51 speak of "the reproach (oneidismos) of your servants" with which enemies taunted "the exchange of your christ" (tou christou sou, "your anointed"). Hebrews says Moses "considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt" (Hebrews 11:26, fresh rendering), and the wording is very close to the Greek of this verse. The writer seems to read Israel's suffering for God's anointed as sharing in Christ's. Compare Romans 15:3, citing 69:9: "The insults of those who insulted you fell on me."

a: Blessed be the LORD forever.
p: This blessing is not part of Psalm 89. It closes Book III, as 41:13, 72:18–19 and 106:48 close the others.
b: Each of the first four books of the Psalter ends with a doxology, a short blessing of God with "Amen" (41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48); Psalm 150 closes the fifth. They are the editors' work, and the Plain gives them the same English where the Hebrew is the same: baruch YHWH, "Blessed be the LORD" (41:13; 72:18; 106:48). Ibn Ezra reports that a great Spanish scholar thought the first scribe wrote it, the way scribes ended a book with a blessing. The Targum doubles it, "Blessed be the name of the LORD in this world... in the world to come", and the Jewish evening service begins a group of verses with it. Placed here, it means the community blesses God even with the question of verses 46–51 unanswered.

a: Amen and amen
p: Amen comes from the root of emunah, "faithfulness", the psalm's key word. It means "surely, so be it".
b: Amen means "firm, sure", and as a response "so be it". It shares the root 'mn with emunah, "faithfulness", and ne'eman, "reliable" (89:28, 37). After a psalm that asks whether God's word is sure, the last word affirms that it is. The Greek renders "may it be, may it be" (genoito genoito). Revelation calls Jesus "the Amen" and "the faithful and true witness" (Revelation 3:14), combining this word with the witness of 89:37.

a: you have raged at your anointed one
t: Claude's theory: the two Ezrahites end Book III
p: Book III ends with Heman's personal darkness and Ethan's national darkness, the two sages Solomon outdid.
b: This is Claude's suggestion. 1 Kings 4:31 names Ethan and Heman, both Ezrahites, as the wise men Solomon surpassed. Psalms 88 and 89, the only psalms credited to them, stand side by side at the end of Book III. One gives a single sufferer's night with no answer; the other gives the nation's: the Davidic promise apparently broken. Perhaps the editors chose, on purpose, the names of the wise whom Solomon surpassed to voice the questions that royal wisdom could not answer, just before Book IV turns to Moses (90:0) and to "The LORD reigns". The pairing of 88 and 89 is often noted (for example by Hossfeld and Zenger); the link to 1 Kings 4:31 as a motive for the placement is Claude's own.

a: Ring out your joy to God, our strength!
p: A scroll from Masada holds most of Psalms 81–85. Qumran fragments hold parts of 86, 88 and 89.
b: Masada. The Masada Psalms scroll (MasPs-a, Mas 1e), copied in the first century BC and found in 1964, preserves roughly 81:2 to 85:6. Its editor, Shemaryahu Talmon, reports that it agrees closely with the Masoretic Text, differing mainly in spelling, which is evidence that the Hebrew of these psalms was already stable. Qumran. 4QPs-e (4Q87) preserves bits of Psalms 76–89, and 4Q236 (4QPs89) is a short copy of 89:20–31 that differs from the Masoretic Text in order and wording; see 89:20. What was checked here: these scroll readings are reported from Talmon, Flint and the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; the scrolls and their DJD editions were not seen. The Greek (Swete's Vaticanus), both Latin Psalters of Jerome, the Targum, Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Midrash Tehillim were checked directly; Syriac and Hebrew-manuscript readings are given as reported in BHS.

a: I have found David my servant
t: A different copy of the oracle at Qumran
p: 4Q236 holds 89:20–31 in a shorter, rearranged form. Some think it older than the Masoretic Text.
b: The Qumran fragment 4Q236 (also called 4QPs89 or 4QPs-x, first century BC) contains only the oracle, 89:20–31, with lines in a different order and shorter wording than the Masoretic Text. Patrick Skehan argued that it preserves an early, shorter form of the oracle, which would support the view that the promise to David circulated by itself before the hymn and the lament were joined to it (compare Clifford). Others, including Peter Flint, think it is an excerpt or a free copy made for study or worship. Its readings are reported here from Flint and the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; the fragment was not seen. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text.
